lead: An engine makes two powers at once: indicated power at the piston face and brake power at the shaft. Only brake power can be measured directly with a brake. Indicated power comes from the p-V loop or from a Morse test. Friction power comes from the motoring test or Willan's line, or by subtraction once IP and BP are known. Test cells use these routes every day to report mechanical efficiency.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for the power and efficiency definitions, and Unit 1 for the working cycle and swept volume.

blocks.text: Power leaves an engine down the shaft. The gas first spends part of its work on the engine's own friction — bearings, rings, valve train, oil and water pumps — and only the remainder reaches the shaft. Three numbers therefore exist.

Indicated power IP is the rate of work done by the gas on the piston. Brake power BP is the rate of work at the shaft. Friction power FP is the difference, and mechanical efficiency is the ratio of the two.
FP = IP − BP          η_mech = BP / IP
blocks.where: IP, BP and FP are in the same unit, usually kW; η_mech is a pure number, often given as a percentage.

blocks.text: Brake power is computed from two measured quantities, torque and speed.

blocks.where: BP is brake power in W; T is the torque absorbed by the dynamometer in N·m; N is engine speed in rev/min; the factor 2π/60 converts rev/min to rad/s. Divide by 1000 for kW.

blocks.text: Torque and speed are read directly, so BP is never in doubt. IP needs a pressure record. FP is not measured at all — it is what remains. See 5.4 for the dynamometer and 5.1 for the rest of the performance parameters.

sections.h3: Indicated power from the p-V loop

items: Record cylinder pressure against volume for one full cycle of one cylinder.
The area inside the closed loop is the net work per cycle, to the pressure and volume scales.
Measure the area in mm² with a planimeter, or count squares.
Divide the area by the diagram length in mm to get the mean height in mm.
Multiply the mean height by the indicator spring constant in bar/mm or kPa/mm. That is the imep.

blocks.where: imep is indicated mean effective pressure in kPa; V_d is swept volume of one cylinder in m³; N is speed in rev/min; n_R is 2 for a four-stroke and 1 for a two-stroke; IP is in kW for one cylinder. Multiply by the number of cylinders.

blocks.text: n_R is the number of revolutions per power stroke. A four-stroke fires once in two revolutions, so at the same speed and imep it gives half the power of a two-stroke.

The old mechanical indicator scratched a diagram on a card; a modern engine uses a piezoelectric transducer and crank-angle encoder to draw the same loop in software (see 5.8). On a four-stroke the pumping loop already lies inside the closed area, so the imep obtained is the net imep.

sections.h3: Morse test: cut one cylinder at a time

blocks.text: The Morse test works on engines with three or more cylinders. Hold speed and load fixed and note BP with all cylinders firing. Cut the ignition (SI) or fuel (CI) of cylinder 1 only, and restore load to bring speed back to the same value. Note the new BP. Repeat for every cylinder.

blocks.where: BP is brake power with all k cylinders firing in kW; BP_i is brake power with cylinder i cut in kW; the drop BP − BP_i is the indicated power of that one cylinder.

items: Assumption 1: friction power is the same whether a cylinder fires or not.
Assumption 2: the firing cylinders deliver the same power as before the cut.
Assumption 3: speed and load are held constant.
Then FP = IP − BP and η_mech = BP/IP. FP must come out small and positive.
Weakness: it needs a multi-cylinder engine, and the cut cylinder cools and loses its oil film.

blocks.text: The motoring test measures friction directly. Couple the engine to a dynamometer, switch off fuel and ignition, and drive it at the test speed. The dynamometer then reads the power needed to turn it over, which is the friction power. It is quick and works on a single-cylinder engine. Weakness: with no combustion the walls, piston and oil are cooler and no gas pressure pushes the rings out, so the friction measured is not the friction at running temperature.

Willan's line uses fuel flow. Hold speed constant and vary the load. Plot fuel consumption rate in kg/h against BP in kW. At moderate and heavy load the points lie on a straight line. Extend it to zero fuel flow: it meets the BP axis at BP = −FP, so the size of that negative intercept is FP. The assumptions are a straight line and friction power independent of load. Near zero load the line curves because combustion becomes poor, so only the straight part may be extrapolated. See 5.3 for the fuel-flow measurement.

figure.caption: Dynamometer torque gives brake power directly; the Morse test builds indicated power from measured brake-power drops; friction power is the difference.

spec.title: Two routes to the three powers

nodes.label: Morse test
nodes.note: cut one cylinder at a time

spec.aria: Block diagram: dynamometer torque gives brake power, the Morse test gives indicated power from brake-power drops, and friction power is the difference.

examples.question: A four-cylinder four-stroke petrol engine runs at constant speed. BP with all four cylinders firing is 20.0 kW. Cutting each cylinder in turn and restoring the same speed gives brake powers 14.2, 14.0, 14.3 and 14.1 kW. Find IP, FP and mechanical efficiency.
steps: Cylinder 1 cut: drop = BP − BP₁ = 20.0 − 14.2 = 5.8 kW, so cylinder 1 indicates 5.8 kW.
Friction power FP = IP − BP = 23.4 − 20.0 = 3.4 kW.
examples.answer: IP = 23.4 kW, FP = 3.4 kW and η_mech = 85.5 %.
examples.check:
bp = 20.0
cut = [14.2, 14.0, 14.3, 14.1]
drops = [round(bp - c, 1) for c in cut]
ip = round(sum(drops), 1)
fp = round(ip - bp, 1)
eta = round(100 * bp / ip, 1)
print(ip)
print(fp)
print(eta)

traps: Adding the four cut readings (56.6 kW) instead of the four drops. A cut reading still contains the brake power of the other cylinders.
Reporting a negative friction power. FP is small and positive; a negative value means a cut reading was copied wrongly or BP was noted with the wrong number of cylinders firing.
Using N instead of N/2 in the indicated power formula for a four-stroke. That doubles IP, so the efficiency you calculate is half the true value: the 85.5 % example would come out near 43 %.
Mixing units in IP = imep × V_d × N/(60 n_R). Use kPa with m³, or convert bar to kPa (×100) and litres to m³ (×10⁻³).
Confusing the three routes: the motoring test gives FP directly, the Morse test gives IP, and Willan's line gives FP by extrapolation of a fuel-flow plot.

quiz.q: Define indicated power, brake power and friction power in one line each.
quiz.a: IP is the rate of work by the gas on the piston; BP is the rate of work at the shaft; FP is IP − BP, the power spent on the engine's own friction and auxiliary drives.

quiz.q: Why can friction power not be measured directly on a firing engine?
quiz.a: Friction acts between moving surfaces inside a running engine and cannot be separated by an instrument. The indicator diagram gives IP only. FP comes by subtraction (IP − BP) or by removing combustion, as in the motoring test.

quiz.q: A single-cylinder four-stroke engine has a swept volume of 0.0006 m³ and runs at 2400 rev/min. The imep from its indicator diagram is 700 kPa. Find the indicated power.
A six-cylinder engine develops 90.0 kW with all cylinders firing. Cutting cylinders in turn gives 71.0, 70.5, 71.5, 70.8, 71.2 and 71.0 kW. Find IP, FP and mechanical efficiency.
A Willan's line at constant speed meets the brake power axis at −2.6 kW. What does this tell you, and why does the line curve near zero load?
quiz.a: The magnitude of the negative intercept is the friction power, so FP = 2.6 kW. At very light load the mixture is poor and a large share of the fuel goes on losses that do not scale with power, so the straight-line law fails.

quiz.q: The motoring test on a cold engine gives a higher friction power than the Morse test on the same warm engine. Give two reasons.
quiz.a: Cold oil is more viscous, so bearing, piston and ring friction is larger. Cooler walls also keep the oil film colder and thicker, raising friction further. Note that the missing gas pressure behind the rings works the other way and tends to lower friction — that is why a motoring test on a warm engine usually reads slightly less than the true running friction.

quiz.q: State the three assumptions of the Morse test.
quiz.a: Friction power is unchanged when a cylinder is cut; the firing cylinders deliver the same indicated power as before the cut; speed and load are held constant throughout.

beyond: Not for the exam. Engine plants run an automated motoring test at the end of the line: the dynamometer spins the engine without fuel and compares the torque trace with a stored signature, catching a tight bearing or wrong cam timing before dispatch. Research engines compute imep cylinder by cylinder, and the cycle-to-cycle spread of imep measures combustion quality. Electric drivetrains use the same idea as a spin-loss test. Search for 'motoring friction test', 'COV of imep' and 'Willan's line extrapolation'.
